claim: Widefield fluorescence microscopy is used to monitor the spiking of populations of neurons in the brain.
source: Widefield fluorescence microscopy is used to monitor the spiking of populations of neurons in the brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the application of widefield fluorescence microscopy, drawing from established scientific practice.

claim: Widefield fluorescence can originate from indicator molecules at all depths in cortex.
source: Widefield fluorescence can originate from indicator molecules at all depths in cortex and the relative contributions from somata, dendrites, and axons are often unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of widefield fluorescence, based on the author's simulation work presented in the manuscript.

claim: The relative contributions from somata, dendrites, and axons to widefield fluorescence are often unknown.
source: Widefield fluorescence can originate from indicator molecules at all depths in cortex and the relative contributions from somata, dendrites, and axons are often unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Scattering strongly affects illumination and collection in widefield fluorescence microscopy.
source: Scattering strongly affects illumination and collection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Illumination intensity is greatest ~300–400 µm below the pia, not at the brain surface.
source: One consequence is that illumination intensity is greatest ~300–400 µm below the pia, not at the brain surface.
evidence: This is a direct result from the Monte Carlo simulation presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fluorescence from a source deep in cortex may extend across a diameter of 3–4 mm at the brain surface.
source: Another is that fluorescence from a source deep in cortex may extend across a diameter of 3–4 mm at the brain surface, severely limiting lateral resolution.
evidence: This is a direct result from the Monte Carlo simulation presented in the manuscript.

claim: The large spread of fluorescence from deep sources severely limits lateral resolution in widefield microscopy.
source: Another is that fluorescence from a source deep in cortex may extend across a diameter of 3–4 mm at the brain surface, severely limiting lateral resolution.

claim: In many mouse lines, the volume of tissue contributing to fluorescence extends through the full depth of cortex.
source: In many mouse lines, the volume of tissue contributing to fluorescence extends through the full depth of cortex and fluorescence at most surface locations is a weighted average across multiple cortical columns and often more than one cortical area.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from combining expression patterns with simulation results.

claim: Fluorescence at most surface locations is a weighted average across multiple cortical columns and often more than one cortical area.
source: In many mouse lines, the volume of tissue contributing to fluorescence extends through the full depth of cortex and fluorescence at most surface locations is a weighted average across multiple cortical columns and often more than one cortical area.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results about the volume of tissue contributing to fluorescence.

claim: Widefield fluorescence microscopy is a popular technique for monitoring activity in the mouse neocortex.
source: Widefield fluorescence microscopy is a popular technique for monitoring activity in the mouse neocortex, often used in combination with genetically-encoded calcium indicators (Mohajerani et al., 2013; Wekselblatt et al., 2016; Allen et al., 2017; Makino et al., 2017; Mitra et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Widefield fluorescence microscopy is often used in combination with genetically-encoded calcium indicators.
source: Widefield fluorescence microscopy is a popular technique for monitoring activity in the mouse neocortex, often used in combination with genetically-encoded calcium indicators (Mohajerani et al., 2013; Wekselblatt et al., 2016; Allen et al., 2017; Makino et al., 2017; Mitra et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: A defining characteristic of widefield microscopes is a lack of optical sectioning.
source: A defining characteristic of widefield microscopes is a lack of optical sectioning.
evidence: This is a statement about the fundamental properties of widefield microscopy, based on established knowledge.

claim: In some mouse lines, fluorescent indicator molecules are expressed at many depths in neocortex.
source: In some mouse lines, fluorescent indicator molecules are expressed at many depths in neocortex, either in multiple cell populations or throughout neurons that extend across cortical layers (Daigle et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Fluorescence can arise from multiple cortical layers in widefield microscopy with no optical sectioning.
source: With no optical sectioning, fluorescence can and often does arise from multiple cortical layers and assignment of the signal to cellular or laminar populations is challenging (Allen et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge about widefield microscopy.

claim: Assignment of widefield fluorescence signal to cellular or laminar populations is challenging.
source: With no optical sectioning, fluorescence can and often does arise from multiple cortical layers and assignment of the signal to cellular or laminar populations is challenging (Allen et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Scattering by brain tissue commonly deflects photons en route to the camera chip, affecting lateral resolution.
source: In addition, scattering by brain tissue commonly deflects photons en route to the camera chip, affecting lateral resolution (Silasi et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Monte Carlo random-walk models provide an accurate and computationally tractable solution to the radiative transport equation.
source: Monte Carlo random-walk models provide an accurate and computationally tractable solution to the radiative transport equation and have been used extensively to simulate the propagation of photons through scattering media, such as biological tissues (Zhu and Liu, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Monte Carlo random-walk models have been used extensively to simulate the propagation of photons through scattering media, such as biological tissues.
source: Monte Carlo random-walk models provide an accurate and computationally tractable solution to the radiative transport equation and have been used extensively to simulate the propagation of photons through scattering media, such as biological tissues (Zhu and Liu, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Random-walk simulations of near-infrared light propagation have been used to refine light intensity, source geometry and duty cycle in photodynamic therapies.
source: Random-walk simulations of near-infrared light propagation have been used to refine light intensity, source geometry and duty cycle in photodynamic therapies (De Jode, 2000; Valentine et al., 2012) and optimize illumination parameters and estimate the volume of tissue contributing to signals in diffuse reflectance tomography (Boas et al., 2002; Fukui et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Random-walk simulations have been used to optimize illumination parameters and estimate the volume of tissue contributing to signals in diffuse reflectance tomography.
source: Random-walk simulations of near-infrared light propagation have been used to refine light intensity, source geometry and duty cycle in photodynamic therapies (De Jode, 2000; Valentine et al., 2012) and optimize illumination parameters and estimate the volume of tissue contributing to signals in diffuse reflectance tomography (Boas et al., 2002; Fukui et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Random-walk models have been used to explore brain illumination in the visible spectrum, often near the tips of optical fibers implanted to activate or silence neurons expressing opsins.
source: More recently, random-walk models have been used to explore brain illumination in the visible spectrum, often near the tips of optical fibers implanted to activate or silence neurons expressing opsins.
evidence: This statement describes recent applications of random-walk models, drawing from established literature.

claim: Random-walk models can accurately predict the volume of tissue in which neurons are activated or silenced.
source: Random-walk models can accurately predict the volume of tissue in which neurons are activated or silenced and have been used to refine stimulation parameters to minimize heating (Bernstein et al., 2008; Kahn et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2015; Stujenske et al., 2015; Yona et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Random-walk models have been used to refine stimulation parameters to minimize heating.
source: Random-walk models can accurately predict the volume of tissue in which neurons are activated or silenced and have been used to refine stimulation parameters to minimize heating (Bernstein et al., 2008; Kahn et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2015; Stujenske et al., 2015; Yona et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Fluorescence has been simulated by separating illumination and the fluorescence detection into two processes.
source: Fluorescence has been simulated by separating illumination and the fluorescence detection into two processes (Chen et al., 2012; Holt et al., 2015; Hennig et al., 2016) and widefield fluorescence has been studied for columnar arrangements of fluorophores, revealing that the effects of numerical aperture and focal position within the tissue depend on the size of the column (Tian et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Widefield fluorescence has been studied for columnar arrangements of fluorophores, revealing that the effects of numerical aperture and focal position within the tissue depend on the size of the column.
source: Fluorescence has been simulated by separating illumination and the fluorescence detection into two processes (Chen et al., 2012; Holt et al., 2015; Hennig et al., 2016) and widefield fluorescence has been studied for columnar arrangements of fluorophores, revealing that the effects of numerical aperture and focal position within the tissue depend on the size of the column (Tian et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The author adapted code previously used to model illumination by visible and near-IR illumination.
source: Here, I adapted code previously used to model illumination by visible and near-IR illumination (Stujenske et al., 2015; Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016; Wang et al., 2020), simulating illumination and fluorescence emission at visible wavelengths in a ~200 mm3 volume of mouse grey matter.
evidence: This statement describes the methodology used in the study, with citations to the original code sources.

claim: The author simulated illumination and fluorescence emission at visible wavelengths in a ~200 mm3 volume of mouse grey matter.
source: Here, I adapted code previously used to model illumination by visible and near-IR illumination (Stujenske et al., 2015; Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016; Wang et al., 2020), simulating illumination and fluorescence emission at visible wavelengths in a ~200 mm3 volume of mouse grey matter.
evidence: This statement describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Spatially detailed models, containing individual tissue elements such as neurons and blood vessels, have proven invaluable for exploring optics with single-neuron resolution.
source: Spatially detailed models, containing individual tissue elements such as neurons and blood vessels, have proven invaluable for exploring optics with single-neuron resolution (Charles et al., 2019), but require substantial computational resources.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Spatially detailed models require substantial computational resources.
source: Spatially detailed models, containing individual tissue elements such as neurons and blood vessels, have proven invaluable for exploring optics with single-neuron resolution (Charles et al., 2019), but require substantial computational resources.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about computational modeling.

claim: The author modeled tissue as a spatially homogenous medium with wavelength-dependent scattering and absorption.
source: I therefore modeled tissue as a spatially homogenous medium with wavelength-dependent scattering and absorption (Wang et al., 1995), a common simplification that requires fewer computational resources and has proven accurate where, as here, many photons propagate for multiple scattering lengths.
evidence: This statement describes the methodology used in the study, with a citation to the modeling approach.

claim: Modeling tissue as a spatially homogenous medium is a common simplification that requires fewer computational resources.
source: I therefore modeled tissue as a spatially homogenous medium with wavelength-dependent scattering and absorption (Wang et al., 1995), a common simplification that requires fewer computational resources and has proven accurate where, as here, many photons propagate for multiple scattering lengths.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about computational modeling approaches.

claim: The homogenous medium model has proven accurate where many photons propagate for multiple scattering lengths.
source: I therefore modeled tissue as a spatially homogenous medium with wavelength-dependent scattering and absorption (Wang et al., 1995), a common simplification that requires fewer computational resources and has proven accurate where, as here, many photons propagate for multiple scattering lengths.

claim: Widefield fluorescence begins with photons, usually from an incoherent source, propagating through the brain surface and into tissue.
source: Widefield fluorescence begins with photons, usually from an incoherent source, propagating through the brain surface and into tissue.
evidence: This statement describes the physical process of widefield fluorescence, based on established knowledge.

claim: Illumination is attenuated by tissue absorption and scattering.
source: This illumination is attenuated by tissue absorption and scattering, and one might expect illumination intensity to decline with depth.
evidence: This statement describes the physical process of light propagation in tissue, based on established knowledge.

claim: After excitation, fluorescence photons propagate from the source molecule in random directions.
source: After excitation, fluorescence photons propagate from the source molecule in random directions.
evidence: This statement describes the physical process of fluorescence emission, based on established knowledge.

claim: Emitted fluorescence is subject to absorption and scattering before exiting the brain.
source: Emitted fluorescence is subject to absorption and scattering before exiting the brain and being focused by the objective onto a detector, usually a camera.
evidence: This statement describes the physical process of fluorescence propagation in tissue, based on established knowledge.

claim: The broad trend of illumination intensity is a decline with tissue depth but with an increase in intensity over the initial 200 µm.
source: As expected, the broad trend was of a decline in illumination intensity with tissue depth but with an increase in intensity over the initial 200 µm (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is directly supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: When the scattering coefficient is set to zero, intensity declines exponentially from the tissue surface with a length constant matching that of absorption.
source: When the scattering coefficient was set to zero, eliminating scattering from the model, intensity declined exponentially from the tissue surface with a length constant matching that of absorption (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is directly supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: With the absorption coefficient set to zero, the superficial rise in intensity becomes larger and extends deeper into the tissue.
source: With the absorption coefficient set to zero, leaving scattering the only mechanism of attenuation, the superficial rise in intensity became larger and extended deeper into the tissue, indicating that the superficial increase in illumination intensity is a result of scattering (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is directly supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The superficial increase in illumination intensity is a result of scattering.
source: With the absorption coefficient set to zero, leaving scattering the only mechanism of attenuation, the superficial rise in intensity became larger and extended deeper into the tissue, indicating that the superficial increase in illumination intensity is a result of scattering (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results comparing conditions with and without scattering.

claim: Photons exit the objective and enter the tissue propagating almost perpendicular to the brain surface.
source: Photons exit the objective and enter the tissue propagating almost perpendicular to the brain surface (Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is directly supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The propagation angle is randomized over multiple scattering events.
source: The propagation angle is randomized over multiple scattering events.
evidence: This statement describes the physical process of light scattering, based on established knowledge and simulation results.

claim: The cosine of the mean angle of propagation relaxes towards zero over ~800 µm.
source: The cosine of the mean angle of propagation (relative to the optical axis; perpendicular to the tissue surface) relaxes towards zero over ~800 µm (Figure 1C), consistent with a calculated transport length of 826 µm.
evidence: This statement is directly supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The relaxation of the cosine of the mean angle of propagation over ~800 µm is consistent with a calculated transport length of 826 µm.
source: The cosine of the mean angle of propagation (relative to the optical axis; perpendicular to the tissue surface) relaxes towards zero over ~800 µm (Figure 1C), consistent with a calculated transport length of 826 µm.
evidence: This is an inference comparing simulation results with calculated values.

claim: By randomizing propagation directions, scattering slows propagation perpendicular to the brain surface, concentrating photons.
source: By randomizing propagation directions, scattering slows propagation perpendicular to the brain surface, concentrating photons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results about how scattering affects photon propagation.

claim: The concentrating effect of scattering is lost when angles at the brain surface are randomized, such as by overlying skull.
source: The concentrating effect of scattering is lost when angles at the brain surface are randomized, such as by overlying skull.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results comparing conditions with and without skull.

claim: In mouse, widefield imaging is often performed through intact skull.
source: In mouse, widefield imaging is often performed through intact skull (Mohajerani et al., 2013; Silasi et al., 2016; Allen et al., 2017; Makino et al., 2017; Gilad and Helmchen, 2020; Valley et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Mouse skull is ~150–300 µm thick.
source: Mouse skull is ~150–300 µm thick and transparent but strongly scattering (Soleimanzad et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Mouse skull is transparent but strongly scattering.
source: Mouse skull is ~150–300 µm thick and transparent but strongly scattering (Soleimanzad et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018).

claim: 300 µm of skull overlaying cortex randomizes the directions of propagation.
source: 300 µm of skull overlaying cortex randomizes the directions of propagation (Figure 1C), eliminating the increase in intensity in superficial tissue (Figure 1D).

claim: 300 µm of skull eliminates the increase in intensity in superficial tissue.
source: 300 µm of skull overlaying cortex randomizes the directions of propagation (Figure 1C), eliminating the increase in intensity in superficial tissue (Figure 1D).
evidence: This statement is directly supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: By randomizing the propagation angles of photons arriving at the brain surface, skull weights excitation towards the most superficial fluorophore molecules.
source: By randomizing the propagation angles of photons arriving at the brain surface, skull weights excitation towards the most superficial fluorophore molecules (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results about the effect of skull on illumination.

claim: 0.58% of photons from a surface source are collected.
source: 0.58% of photons from a surface source are collected (Figure 2B).

claim: The collection percentage increases slightly with source depth to ~400 µm, due to scattering, and decreases thereafter.
source: The collection percentage increases slightly with source depth to ~400 µm, due to scattering, and decreases thereafter (Figure 2B).

claim: Photons from deep within cortex can contribute as much to detected fluorescence as photons from superficial layers.
source: Photons from deep within cortex can contribute as much to detected fluorescence as photons from superficial layers, with collection percentages for sources on the surface and 1 mm deep being equal.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results about collection efficiency at different depths.

claim: Collection percentages for sources on the surface and 1 mm deep are equal.
source: Photons from deep within cortex can contribute as much to detected fluorescence as photons from superficial layers, with collection percentages for sources on the surface and 1 mm deep being equal.

claim: Collected photons are scattered en route to the tissue surface.
source: Collected photons are scattered en route to the tissue surface.

claim: Photons from a point source in the tissue form a patch of fluorescence on the surface.
source: Photons from a point source in the tissue form a patch of fluorescence on the surface (Figure 2A).

claim: The diameter of the fluorescence patch is greater for sources at depth than near the surface.

claim: The diameter containing 50% of photons is 10 µm for a source on the brain surface and 860 µm for a 1 mm deep source.
source: The diameter containing 50% of photons is 10 µm for a source on the brain surface and 860 µm for a 1 mm deep source; the diameter containing 95% of photons is 2.6 mm for a source on the brain surface and 3.9 mm for a 1 mm deep source (Figure 2C).

claim: The diameter containing 95% of photons is 2.6 mm for a source on the brain surface and 3.9 mm for a 1 mm deep source.

claim: Nearby sources, even in the superficial layers of cortex, produce overlapping surface distributions.
source: Nearby sources, even in the superficial layers of cortex, produce overlapping surface distributions.

claim: The model accurately predicted the surface distribution of photons.

claim: The model slightly overestimated the spread toward the edges, but accurately predicted the distribution of the majority of photons.
source: The model slightly overestimated the spread toward the edges, but accurately predicted the distribution of the majority of photons (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental validation shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: Changing the depth of the focal plane below the tissue surface has no effect on illumination.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3A, changing the depth of the focal plane below the tissue surface has no effect on illumination, the percentage of photons collected from different depths, or the distribution of fluorescence at the tissue surface (though, of course, adjusting the focus will change the distribution of photons on the camera chip).
evidence: This statement is directly supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Changing the depth of the focal plane has no effect on the percentage of photons collected from different depths.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3A, changing the depth of the focal plane below the tissue surface has no effect on illumination, the percentage of photons collected from different depths, or the distribution of fluorescence at the tissue surface (though, of course, adjusting the focus will change the distribution of photons on the camera chip).

claim: Adjusting the focus will change the distribution of photons on the camera chip.

evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about optical imaging.

claim: The lack of effect of changing the focal plane is consistent with the results of Tian et al., 2011.
source: The lack of effect of changing the focal plane is consistent with the results of Tian et al., 2011, who found that focal plane depth mattered little when imaging large regions of uniform fluorescence, and also considered the effects of focal plane on the distribution of photons on the camera chip.

claim: Tian et al., 2011 found that focal plane depth mattered little when imaging large regions of uniform fluorescence.

claim: Peak illumination intensity and collection efficiency remains at ~0.3–0.4 mm below the tissue surface, in superficial layers of cortex, across a range of numerical apertures.

claim: The lack of effect of NA is consistent with published results.
source: The lack of effect of NA is consistent with published results (Tian et al., 2011).

claim: Reducing the field of view from 11 to 4.4 mm has no effect on illumination.
source: Reducing the field of view from 11 to 4.4 mm (corresponding to an increase in objective magnification from x2 to x10; TL2X-SAP and TL10X-2P objectives) has no effect on illumination (Figure 3C) but reduces collection efficiency and the diameter of surface distribution of fluorescence (Figure 3C).
evidence: This statement is directly supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Reducing the field of view from 11 to 4.4 mm reduces collection efficiency.
source: Reducing the field of view from 11 to 4.4 mm (corresponding to an increase in objective magnification from x2 to x10; TL2X-SAP and TL10X-2P objectives) has no effect on illumination (Figure 3C) but reduces collection efficiency and the diameter of surface distribution of fluorescence (Figure 3C).
evidence: This statement is directly supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Reducing the field of view from 11 to 4.4 mm reduces the diameter of surface distribution of fluorescence.

claim: Even a microscope objective with a fairly large field of view can cause vignetting.
source: These results illustrate one consequence of the large surface distribution of fluorescence: even a microscope objective with a fairly large field of view can cause vignetting.

claim: Skull weights illumination and fluorescence collection towards deeper layers of cortex.
source: Finally, I examined the consequences of imaging through 300 µm of skull. Skull weights illumination and fluorescence collection towards deeper layers of cortex (Figure 1D, Figure 3D) and slightly broadens the central peak of the surface fluorescence distribution (Figure 3D).
evidence: This statement is directly supported by simulation results shown in Figures 1D and 3D.

claim: Skull slightly broadens the central peak of the surface fluorescence distribution.

claim: Optical parameters typically have modest effects on widefield fluorescence.

claim: Changing to a higher magnification objective will generally result in a greater numerical aperture and a smaller field of view.

claim: The absorption and scattering coefficients used in the model were measured in vivo.

claim: The absorption coefficient in vivo is ~5 times greater than that measured in vitro, largely because of absorption by hemoglobin.

source: Nonetheless, in the brain there will be local variations in absorption and scattering, such as in the vicinity of blood vessels, resulting in local effects that are not reflected in Figures 1–3.

claim: 500 µm of blood transmits <<1% of incident light.
source: From the Beer-Lambert law, 500 µm of blood transmits <<1% of incident light but 200 µm of blood transmits ~6% (2.2 × 10−3 mol/L hemoglobin, 50% hemoglobin oxygenation, hemoglobin molar extinction coefficient 27,895 cm−1M−1; Valley et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is calculated from the Beer-Lambert law using parameters from a cited source.

claim: 200 µm of blood transmits ~6% of incident light.
source: From the Beer-Lambert law, 500 µm of blood transmits <<1% of incident light but 200 µm of blood transmits ~6% (2.2 × 10−3 mol/L hemoglobin, 50% hemoglobin oxygenation, hemoglobin molar extinction coefficient 27,895 cm−1M−1; Valley et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is calculated from the Beer-Lambert law using parameters from a cited source.

claim: The simple simulation of blood vessels slightly overestimates the effects of vessels, particularly small vessels.
source: Likely this simple simulation slightly overestimates the effects of vessels, particularly small vessels.

source: Illumination intensity is reduced immediately below a vessel and throughout the deeper cortical tissue, but even tissue immediately under the vessel received substantial illumination (Figure 4A–C).

claim: Even tissue immediately under the vessel received substantial illumination.

claim: Fluorescence collection from under the vessel was reduced but remained substantial.
